The Greeks prized beauty and the Jews holiness, but both peoples loved truth. The Greeks thought deeply about every problem except religion, while the Jews gave themselves wholly to religion. These two streams met in Jesus' message and became the driving force of a new social order (195:1.6).
195:42: Just as Alexander went east carrying Greek culture, Paul went west carrying the Christian version of the gospel. The Eastern version, truer to Jesus' teachings, followed Abner's uncompromising attitude and in the end disappeared into the Islamic movement (195:1.10-1.11).
195:44: Rome brought a new tolerance of foreign languages, peoples, and religions. The early persecutions came because Christians used the word "kingdom" in their preaching and were mistaken for political rivals (195:2.1-2.2). The Romans, honest, devoted, and self-controlled but without a religion worthy of the name, were ideal soil for receiving Christianity (195:2.3-2.4).
195:45: Rome adopted Christ as a moral philosophy, and Christianity became the moral culture of Rome. But for many it did not work as religion in the sense of a personal experience of spiritual growth. Even so, many individuals penetrated beneath the surface of the state religion and found its hidden truths as food for their souls (195:2.5). For the Greeks, who had long believed in survival after death, the teaching of immortality had especially strong appeal (195:2.8).
195:57: The Christians had one God but no empire; the Greco-Romans had an empire but no fitting God. So the Christians accepted the empire, and the empire adopted Christianity (195:3.1). To people who did not even have a word for "unselfishness," Christianity came as a fresh consolation, and the way believers lived and died in service amid persecution became its greatest power (195:3.3-3.4). The teaching that Christ loved little children ended the practice of exposing unwanted babies (195:3.5).
195:66: Unity of religious thought and practice
195:68: But for the Roman Empire Christianity was only a cultural necessity, not a means of spiritual salvation. The book names many causes, such as excessive paternalism, abuses of taxation, a mania for amusement, and a spiritually barren state church, and says that not even a good religion could save the empire (195:3.8-3.9). Nevertheless, by the end of the second century nearly all the great minds of the Greco-Roman world had become Christians (195:3.10).
195:70: Because the church had allied itself with politics, it shared in the decline of the Dark Ages. Religion became monasticized and legalized, and the individual nearly vanished before the authority and traditions of the church. A new menace also arose in the veneration of "saints" who supposedly interceded before the gods (195:4.1-4.2). Still, Christianity was socialized enough to endure this long night and survive to the dawn of the Renaissance (195:4.3).
195:71: The book sums up how, after changing from the religion of Jesus into a religion about Jesus, Christianity passed through Hellenization, paganization, secularization, institutionalization, decline and hibernation, and rebirth and division. This long course shows the amazing vitality and power of recovery within it, and now it faces a greater struggle for survival in an age of scientific thinking and materialism. But the religion of Jesus will finally triumph (195:4.4-4.5).
195:73: The more civilization advances, the more necessary it becomes to "⟦Q 195:5.1⟧seek first the realities of heaven⟦/Q⟧" (195:5.1). Religion is a purely personal and spiritual experience that reveals to man his divine and eternal destiny, and it must be distinguished from other high forms of thought (195:5.3). A social system lacking morality founded on spiritual realities can no more be maintained than a solar system without gravity (195:5.9).
195:80: The contrast of beauty and ugliness
195:87: ⟦Q 195:5.12⟧As you view the world, remember that the black patches of evil which you see are shown against a white background of ultimate good.⟦/Q⟧ (195:5.12)
195:89: The book counsels patience: do not try to satisfy all curiosity and every urge for adventure within one short life (195:5.10). Jesus followed the method of experience in religion just as science follows the method of experiment, and among the love of beauty, the pursuit of truth, loyalty to duty, and the worship of goodness, love is the guide to true insight (195:5.14).
195:91: Scientists have unintentionally thrown mankind into a materialistic panic, but the bank of human experience holds vast spiritual assets. When the panic has passed, it will be seen that the religion of Jesus has never been bankrupt (195:6.1). True religion cannot quarrel with science. What science has destroyed is only the childish illusions that misinterpreted life (195:6.2, 6.4).
195:104: Demonstrates the conservation of the human soul
195:106: A machine cannot know, still less can it know truth, hunger for righteousness, and cherish goodness (195:6.11). Materialism, mechanism, and determinism all exist, but none of them is everything (195:6.14). In every realm of existence freedom and initiative are proportional to spiritual influence, and in man, to the degree of doing the Father's will (195:6.16).
195:108: ⟦Q 195:6.16⟧And so, when you once start out to find God, that is the conclusive proof that God has already found you.⟦/Q⟧ (195:6.16)
195:111: Facts never clash with real spiritual faith, but theories may. Science should strive not to destroy faith but to clear away superstition, and it should do materially what religion does spiritually: widen the horizons of life and enlarge personality (195:7.1-7.2).
195:112: The book points out more than once the self-contradiction of mechanism. If the universe were only matter and man only a machine, that man could never recognize that he was a machine. The self-conscious man who declares himself a mechanist is himself the best answer to mechanism (195:7.3, 7.13). The very pessimism of the most pessimistic materialist is proof that the universe is not only matter, for both pessimism and optimism arise only in a mind conscious of values (195:7.8).
195:117: The reality of the evolving energy and material universe
195:119: The morontia world lying between matter and spirit
195:121: The existence of spirit reality and divine values
195:123: Science lives by the mathematics of the mind, music expresses the tempo of the emotions, and religion is the spiritual rhythm of the soul in harmony with the eternal melody of the Infinite (195:7.20). The universe is more like the curious, thinking, choosing scientist himself than like the laws he has discovered (195:7.22).
195:125: The book calls godless science the father of modern secularism and the totalitarian medieval church its mother. Secularism began as a protest against the church's almost complete domination of Western civilization (195:8.2). It broke the fetters of the church, but it soon handed man over to the political and economic bondage of the totalitarian state (195:8.4).
195:132: Ignores God — lately even seeking to take the place of religion
195:134: The book cautions against hastily throwing away the benefits the secular revolt brought, such as tolerance, social service, democratic government, and civil liberties. There is no need to give up faith in God to enjoy those blessings. The greatest mistake of secularism was that, in revolting against the bondage of the church, it rebelled against God himself (195:8.6, 8.8). The brotherhood of men cannot be built while ignoring or denying the fatherhood of God (195:8.11).
195:136: A paganized and socialized Christianity needs a new contact with the uncompromised teachings of Jesus. It is languishing for want of a new vision of the Master's life on earth (195:9.2). The book says modern people have good reasons for avoiding the religion of Jesus, for it actually transforms the believer and demands that he devote his life to knowing the Father's will and to unselfish service for the brotherhood of man (195:9.6).
195:137: ⟦Q 195:9.8⟧The world needs more firsthand religion.⟦/Q⟧ Today most people experience religion secondhand, as their teachers hand it to them. How the world would awaken if it could know directly the way Jesus actually lived and what he taught (195:9.8)! The modern church, instead of being the dynamic brotherhood of believers Jesus commissioned, is threatened with slow death by formalism and overorganization (195:9.10).
195:139: The world needs to see Jesus living again on earth in the experience of spirit-born mortals. It is futile to talk of a return to primitive Christianity; we must go forward from where we are (195:10.1). God and man need each other, and the saying "the kingdom of God is within you" was perhaps the greatest pronouncement Jesus ever made (195:10.3-10.4).
195:154: The true church, the brotherhood of Jesus, is invisible and spiritual, and it is marked by unity, not uniformity. The living Jesus is the only hope of a unified Christianity (195:10.11). The book sternly criticizes the church's involvement in commerce and politics, yet it says not to despise Christianity, for it has been one of the greatest powers for good (195:10.12-10.13). The hope of modern Christianity lies in humbling itself at the foot of the cross and learning anew the living gospel of the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man (195:10.21).
195:156: Paper 195 looks back over the long history of Christianity with both criticism and respect. Christianity grew by compromise on the foundations of Greek thought and the Roman Empire, survived by enduring the Dark Ages, and now stands before the greater challenges of materialism and secularism. The book says that mechanism refutes itself and that secularism cannot bring peace without God, yet it does not look for the answer in a return to the old church. The answer is Jesus himself. When Jesus lives again in the lives of believers, when people walk the second mile, and when they learn anew the living gospel of the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man, the religion of Jesus will once more show its full power to the world.

196:1: Does following Jesus mean believing in Jesus, or believing together with him as he believed?
196:4: Paper 195 looked back on the history of Christianity spreading as a religion about Jesus and said that what the world most needs now is Jesus himself. Paper 196, the last paper, looks into the faith of that very Jesus. Jesus went through all the ups and downs of life, yet he never religiously doubted God's watchcare. His faith was neither traditional nor merely intellectual; it was wholly personal and purely spiritual, born of the indwelling Adjuster (196:0.1).
196:5: Jesus did not cling to faith as a comfort in despair or a compensation for painful reality. He enjoyed serenity in unquestioning trust in God (196:0.3). His faith was as pure as a child's trust, yet never childish; it was intense, yet never fanatical (196:0.6-0.7, 0.12). For him prayer was not a religious duty but unceasing communion with God (196:0.10).
196:6: So does following Jesus mean believing in Jesus, or believing together with him as he believed?
196:8: Jesus does not require his disciples to believe in him but rather to believe with him. (196:0.13)
196:12: The book says that Jesus' greatest contribution to human experience lay not so much in revealing many new ideas about God as in humanly demonstrating a new and higher living faith in God (196:0.3). He challenges us not only to believe what he believed but also to believe as he believed. This is the full meaning of "Follow me" (196:0.13).
196:13: However great the sovereignty of Michael, it must not take the man Jesus away from people. He was a religious man who knew and did God's will by faith, the most truly religious man who ever lived on Urantia (196:1.1). The book says it is time for the human Jesus, buried in theological tradition, to have a figurative resurrection (196:1.2). The greatest religious teacher in the world was, in fact, a layman (196:1.4).
196:15: ⟦Q 196:1.3⟧Of all human knowledge, that which is of greatest value is to know the religious life of Jesus and how he lived it.⟦/Q⟧ (196:1.3)
196:17: The believer's goal is not to imitate Jesus' outward life literally but to share his faith. Jesus never argued about the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of men. He was a living illustration of the one and a demonstration of the other (196:1.5). And just as man must advance from human consciousness to the realization of divinity, so Jesus ascended from the human to the divine through mortal faith and the work of the Adjuster (196:1.6).
196:24: The messenger of Immanuel who appeared at Jerusalem when he was about twelve
196:28: ⟦Q 196:1.10⟧The experiences on the Mount of Transfiguration⟦/Q⟧
196:34: ⟦Q 196:1.13⟧The final embrace of the Paradise Father, conferring unlimited sovereignty⟦/Q⟧
196:37: A religion about Jesus can be preached, but the religion of Jesus must be lived. The book explains that at Pentecost Peter unintentionally founded a new religion of the risen Christ, and Paul transformed it into Christianity based on his own experience. So the New Testament is a superb Christian document, but it contains very little about Jesus' own religious life (196:2.1).
196:43: The personal religious experience of Jesus of Galilee
196:46: Doing God's will and serving one's brothers
196:50: Fellow believers in the divine Christ
196:52: The Gospels too show different sides of Jesus. Mark, Matthew, and Luke portray to some extent the human Jesus nobly struggling to understand and do the divine will, while John portrays the triumphant Jesus walking the earth in full consciousness of divinity. It was a great mistake to see him either as only human or as only divine. He was truly both human and divine, and he still is (196:2.3). The firm belief of the New Testament writers that the Master would soon return was also related to their tendency to take the purely human Master out of the record (196:2.5).
196:53: In one short life Jesus experienced all the religious progress that people ordinarily attain only at the end of the long pre-Paradise journey. He grew from the humble dependence of "Why do you call me good?" to the sublime consciousness of achieved divinity. This ascent was wholly a mortal achievement, and afterward he was still the same human Jesus (196:2.2). The book says that the greatest mistake was this: the human Jesus was recognized as having a religion, but the divine Christ almost overnight became a religion (196:2.4).
196:54: Jesus led people to feel at home in the world and taught that the world is not fundamentally evil. He did not share Paul's pessimistic view of mankind; he saw people as children of God who are weak rather than wicked, distracted rather than depraved (196:2.9). Many of his seemingly hard sayings were not so much commands to others as pledges of consecration he required of himself (196:2.7).
196:56: Personal, spiritual religious experience is an efficient solvent for most human problems. Religion does not do away with problems, but it dissolves, illuminates, and transcends them (196:3.1). Man is educated by fact, ennobled by wisdom, and saved by religious faith (196:3.4).
196:75: To understand reality ever more fully is to draw nearer to God, and to seek God is to experience self-completion. To experience total reality is to realize God fully (196:3.3). Worship is not a vain self-monologue but personal communion with the source of reality, and God is not an invention of human idealism but the loving personality from whom all manifestations of truth, beauty, and goodness come (196:3.22, 3.24).
196:84: The truth of genuine religious experience
196:90: Able to love unselfishly and unconditionally
196:92: Understanding that the universe is friendly to the individual
196:94: Realizing the divine presence and seeking fuller experience
196:96: The human mind does not create values; it discovers, recognizes, interprets, and chooses them (196:3.10). The moral values of the universe become ours through moral choices, which are self-judgment; ethical choices, which are social judgment; and religious choices, which are God-judgment (196:3.11-3.14). Morality is the indispensable soil of God-consciousness, but it is not the source of religious experience. Religion exalts everything morality approves and guarantees its survival (196:3.25, 3.27).
196:105: A religion of faith, hope, and charity
196:107: A religion of love — security in the Father's love and joy in service
196:109: Love is the highest motivation man can use in his universe ascent, but love without truth, beauty, and goodness is only a sentiment (196:3.29). The greatest challenge for modern man is to achieve better communication with the divine Monitor who dwells within the mind (196:3.34). The book tells us not to be discouraged and says that the revelation of God given in Jesus will not fail (196:3.33).
196:111: ⟦Q 196:3.35⟧When all is said and done, the Father idea is still the highest human concept of God.⟦/Q⟧ (196:3.35)
196:114: At the end of this long book, Paper 196 turns our eyes back to the faith of the human Jesus. Jesus trusted God like a child yet met every trial with the courage of a grown man, and by that faith he ascended from the human to the divine and became a new and living way that every mortal can walk. The book urges us to go beyond a religion about Jesus and return to the religion of Jesus. That means not imitating his outward life, but trusting God as he trusted him and believing in people as he believed in them. When we do this, religion becomes a living experience of security in the Father's love and joy in serving our brothers.
